study_description: A corpus-wide survey of Christian, Gnostic, mystical, apocalyptic, and comparative-religion motifs across Philip K. Dick's novels and short stories.

featured_sections.title: Religion in PKD's fiction
body: Philip K. Dick's fiction keeps returning to the same religious pressure points: false worlds, hidden rulers, saving interventions, and the question of whether reality is a prison, a revelation, or both at once. Early novels such as Eye in the Sky and The Man in the High Castle already treat reality as spiritually unstable; later books like The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, Ubik, and A Maze of Death turn salvation into a battle over counterfeit transcendence; the late VALIS novels make theology explicit and autobiographical.

The fiction is not limited to Christianity. Dick's stories repeatedly weave in Gnostic myth, Pauline and Johannine Christology, apocalypse, Buddhist and Hindu language, Platonic recollection, and comparative religion. Rather than presenting one settled creed, the novels and stories stage a running inquiry into what counts as grace, how revelation arrives, and whether the divine comes as voice, vision, surveillance, or repair.

This study is meant as a reading guide across the canon. It does not flatten the differences between the early social satires, the middle-period metaphysical novels, and the late religious novels; instead, it names the recurring patterns so readers can move between fiction, Exegesis, and biography without losing the thread.
